title: Quantum computer scaling advances
html:
Several quantum computing firms are pushing hard to deliver large-scale systems over the next few years. In the last few weeks, IBM, Quantinuum, PsiQuantum and Universal Quantum have all shown technologies that will scale to thousands of qubits, while researchers are finding new technologies for interconnection and non-volatile memory.

“Quantum computers are on the brink of achieving fault tolerance at scale. It’s exciting: we are entering terra incognita for what we can compute. The new challenge is putting our high-level quantum algorithms into the right form to successfully run on error-corrected hardware,” said José Ignacio Latorre, Director of the Centre for Quantum Technologies, Singapore’s flagship national research centre for quantum technology.

IBM scales connectivity

Modular quantum architectures that combine multiple quantum processor units (QPUs) require long-distance quantum interconnects to stitch together individual processor modules. These interconnects, called long-distance couplers or L-couplers, must support coherent quantum operation over meter-scale distances and scale to multiple connections between any two modules.

Researchers at IBM have shown four L-couplers operating between two 120-qubit IBM Nighthawk R1 superconducting qubit processors in a quantum computer called Flamingo. Each L-coupler joins two Nighthawk lattice qubits through two frequency-tunable L-qubits, two superconducting RF couplers, and 80 cm of superconducting aluminium coax.

To enable intermodule operation with high fidelity, the L-coupler must be low loss and high coherence. A major obstacle is connecting the cable to the processor chip in a way that is compatible with how a large, fully wired processor is built and installed. L-coupler counts are expected to increase substantially over the coming years, which will stress reproducibility, scalability and yield.

Each cable installs perpendicular to the processor surface, to enable denser connections, and is joined to the chip by an indium-to-indium room temperature pressure bond made after both modules were mounted.

These four high-fidelity L-couplers establish a practical path to scalable quantum interconnects for modular quantum computing says the team.

Optical Circuit Switching

PsiQuantum has also recently unveiled its Optical Circuit Switching (OCS) technology, demonstrating how a low-loss silicon photonics platform can be applied to some of the most significant scaling challenges for both quantum computing and AI.

The first publicly disclosed OCS system is an 8×8-radix demonstration vehicle built on the low-loss, silicon photonics platform that the company has spent nearly a decade developing for utility-scale quantum computing. Testing conducted in PsiQuantum’s labs has shown typical results of 1.2 dB of insertion loss, 40 dB cross talk, and less than 3 ms of reconfiguration time, all exceeding initial targets set for these devices and without amplification.

PsiQuantum is now sharing samples of its demonstration vehicle with key customers and is planning commercial products that will be announced in the coming months.

AI and quantum computing are complementary technologies: more efficient AI infrastructure can accelerate the development and operation of quantum systems, while some advances made for quantum computing can help remove bottlenecks in AI infrastructure. As optics make AI infrastructure more efficient, stronger AI infrastructure can in turn support the design, control, and operation of increasingly capable quantum systems.

The 8 x 8 OCS module Image: PsiQuantum

“This opportunity exists because we chose to solve the hardest scaling problems at the beginning of our roadmap to utility-scale quantum computing,” said Victor Peng, Chief Executive Officer of PsiQuantum who was formerly CEO of FPGA-developer Xilinx before its acquisition by AMD. “As AI computing pushes infrastructure to its limits, we now have an opportunity to put our state-of-the-art technology to work today while continuing toward our ultimate goal: building and deploying the world’s first useful, fault-tolerant quantum computers.”

“AI is driving extraordinary growth in the scale and complexity of computing infrastructure, and optics will play an increasingly important role in enabling that growth,” said Rob Soderbery, Executive Vice President at PsiQuantum. “PsiQuantum has spent nearly a decade developing silicon photonics against some of the most demanding requirements imaginable. What we are demonstrating today is that this platform can deliver exceptional performance for optical circuit switching for AI computing.”

PsiQuantum has also developed barium titanate (BTO) integration on 300mm wafers with chip partner GlobalFoundries (GF) and uses a 64×64 BTO switch in its quantum systems. BTO is not required for the demonstration vehicle or initial products announced today, highlighting the performance of the underlying silicon photonics platform while preserving an additional path to faster, more advanced future products.

Molecular qubits

Quantum technology company NVision has also published its research integrating thin-film molecular qubits directly onto advanced photonic integrated circuits (PICs) using standard foundry processes.

The research confirms the first ever individually addressable organic molecular spin-photon interface, which is the key ingredient for connecting stationary qubits with photons. Until now, molecular spins could not be individually and coherently controlled, preventing them from serving as true qubits. This means the qubits can be controlled at the single-molecule level and opens a new path to scale, where molecular qubits can be deposited as thin films, much like OLED materials, directly on top of PICs.

“This proves what we’ve long believed: that organic chemistry offers a fundamentally better building block for quantum,” said Sella Brosh, CEO of NVision. “For years, the industry has been locked in a hardware race using modalities that would require decades and multi-billion-dollar proprietary fabrication facilities to achieve scale. With the creation of the world’s first manufacturable organic qubit, we now enter quantum’s molecular era, establishing a new architecture based on photonic connectivity from the get-go, with a clear path to scale through existing foundry infrastructure.”

Chips have been made by foundry partners and NVision is targeting a live demonstration of on-chip performance on PICs by the end of the year. The long-term commercial roadmap targets 1,000 logical, fault-tolerant qubits on chip by 2030 housed within a deployable form factor.

The Photonic Integrated Quantum Circuit (PIQC) for scalable quantum interconnect Source: Nvision

To achieve this, Nvision is now working with HyperLight, a developer of thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) photonics, to establish a practical path to quantum computing at scale, using photonic connectivity to link quantum resources within and across processors. This opens a path toward millions of qubits on chips compatible with standard foundry manufacturing.

“Integrating NVision’s breakthrough molecular qubits onto our PICs unlocks a compelling path for scalable quantum hardware while showcasing the capabilities and versatility of TFLN technology,” said Kevin Luke, co-founder and Head of Custom Development at HyperLight. “Photonic interconnectivity is essential for scaling quantum processors, and combining our optical chip infrastructure with manufacturable molecular thin films allows us to deliver high-density, chip-scale quantum connectivity that leverages decades of investment in semiconductor fabrication.”

NVision’s Photonic Integrated Quantum Circuit (PIQC) architecture uses optical links to link qubits across larger distances, with the carbene molecules functioning at accessible cryogenic temperatures (2K–4K) and emitting photons natively at precise optical frequencies. This enables direct intra-chip and inter-chip quantum entanglement for larger, scalable systems.

“Chemistry gives us a design freedom that semiconductor-based qubits, such as in silicon, simply do not have. By addressing quantum design at the molecular level, we can tune the performance that matters most, including quantum memory, gate speed and photon emission, within a single molecule,” said Ilai Schwartz, CTO of NVision. “Because our qubits interact directly with light from the start, we achieve connectivity without proximity, making photonic networking a foundational capability of our platform rather than something we have to add later.”

To achieve this, NVision combined large-scale computational screening with targeted synthesis, evaluating more than 150 candidate molecules, out of which 40 were synthesized in the laboratory. The resulting carbene system is engineered to interface directly with photons, making photonic connectivity a practical building block for scalable architectures. Crucially, the platform tolerates up to 70% photon loss, enabling reliable operation with standard silicon photonics rather than requiring ultra-low-loss, specialized optical infrastructure.

Fault-tolerant quantum computers

Meanwhile, US/UK quantum giant Quantinuum has shown its roadmap to a fully fault-tolerant quantum computer with thousands of qubits in 2029, which it says will be the world’s first such system.

The company was formed from the merger of Honeywell’s quantum hardware business and Cambridge Quantum Computing in 2021 to create a ‘full stack’ quantum computer company. The Nexus roadmap introduces new capabilities with each generation of hardware through Sol next year to Apollo in 2029 with both on-premises and cloud access options.

The Sol system will have 192 physical qubits with around 100 logical qubits, which is a significant advancement in fault-tolerance. The Apollo system will have thousands of physical qubits with hundreds of logical qubits as a fully fault-tolerant quantum computer. These

These use trapped-ion qubit technology with barium ions built on a Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (QCCD) architecture. The current Helios system has 98 qubits arranged in a trap with a storage ring and linear gating zones, manipulated with lasers and offering all-to-all connectivity. Sol builds on the same trapped-ion QCCD architecture but with a two-dimensional grid trap to shorten ion transport and cooling times while scaling connectivity.

“Our full-stack approach means each advance in hardware can become a capability customers can build on through Nexus,” said Rajeeb Hazra, CEO of Quantinuum CEO. “Our aim is to build the first developer platform specifically for the fault-tolerant era so customers can start developing applications today and carry that investment forward. Nexus is designed to help them deploy applications and hybrid workflows and integrate the platform into their computing environments. As our systems become more capable, our aim is for the applications, workflows, and expertise customers develop in Nexus to become more valuable, giving them a compelling reason to build with Quantinuum and making Nexus an enduring part of their computing environment.”

The Nexus quantum computer roadmap Source: Quantinuum

The roadmap (above) includes pre-built primitives, fault-tolerant libraries, and domain-specific tools that help developers move from individual quantum circuits to complete applications. The platform will progressively automate error-correction encoding, compilation, and resource management, allowing developers to focus more on the application and less on the underlying hardware complexity. Over 200 organizations are already using the technology, up 45% in 2026.

“Developer platforms like Nexus help us bridge that gap between quantum algorithm design and deployment,” said Latorre. The capabilities are expected to provide a continuous path from early application development on the current Helios quantum computer to increasingly capable implementations on Sol and Apollo to help customers carry their investments forward as the hardware advances.

Developers can write programs, automatically encode them for supported error-correction schemes, test them in emulation, and execute supported programs on Helios. These capabilities establish the foundation for future roadmap releases, including a release next month that will add supported error-correction codes.

iQPU

Universal Quantum in the UK is also using a QCCD architecture, and this month showed its integrated QPU (iQPU) built on a standard 200mm semiconductor line. The iPQU combines the world’s largest trapped-ion compute surface, ultra-low noise integrated control electronics and interfaces that connect multiple iQPUs through a proprietary chip-to-chip technology called UQConnect technology. This enables scaling of the systems.

At the centre of the platform is the iQPU (above). This is a trapped-ion processor chip with an active compute area of more than 400mm² where the QCCD architecture moves ions across the chip. This enables long-range connections between qubits rather than fixing each qubit to a single location, reducing the number of qubits required to solve commercial problems and speeding up computations.

Manufacturing on a standard chip process matters because scaling quantum computers requires more than a larger experimental device: it requires components that can be produced repeatedly and at low cost, tested reliably and integrated through mature supply chains.

“The question is no longer whether quantum computing can work, but how we build enough high-quality qubits to solve problems that matter,” said Sebastian Weidt, CEO and Co-Founder of Universal Quantum. “The iQPU allows us to combine our world record interconnect technology with a chip architecture that can control qubits at scale and is manufactured in commercial silicon foundries. It opens up an exciting route for us from today’s systems to the utility-scale quantum computers the world needs.”

The iQPU will be integrated into systems currently being delivered to customers including the German Aerospace Center (DLR).

Research

Researchers at Quantum Motion in London, as well as University College London, Imperial College London, the University of Cambridge, CIC nanoGUNE in San Sebastián, and the Basque Foundation for Science have created integrated superinductors for quantum systems using standard 22nm process technology from GF.

The films of TiN, which become superconducting at deep-cryogenic temperatures, are found in the poly-resistors of the 22nm fully depleted silicon-on-insulator process to create radiofrequency single-electron transistors that are widely used as sensors in semiconductor-based quantum computers.

Quantum Motion worked with HRL Laboratories, now part of IBM, Diraq and Intel, other companies that are looking to develop quantum computers using semiconductor spin qubits. The sensors are created by integrating a resonator containing the superinductor and a silicon quantum dot formed within the same integrated circuit. The resulting system has a footprint of only 18 μm2 and offers a power signal-to-noise ratio of 4,500 in an integration time of 4 ns.

“The finding that TiN in an unmodified, off-the-shelf CMOS metallization achieves superinductor-grade performance and without any process engineering for that purpose is genuinely unexpected and fortuitous,” said Thaddeus Ladd, Chief Scientist of the Computational Physics Division at HRL Laboratories.

At the same time, Dr Stavroula Kapoulea, Cofounder of Kelvin Quantum in Glasgow, Scotland, is leading a UK project to design and deploy ultra-cold semiconductor electronics for quantum applications.

The £1.65M CONQRETE project is focusing on scalability. The goal is to bring quantum control and readout electronics into the ultra-cold environment where qubits operate to unlock scalable, practical quantum computing.

The project will work alongside partners from National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC), National Physical Laboratory (NPL), the Semiconductor Catapult, and Keysight Technologies to develop advanced cryogenic microchips and packaging, along with the control software and measurement capabilities needed to bring everything together into a fully integrated system.

SemiQoN in Espoo, FInaland, is also working on memory technology that can be used in superconducting quantum systems.

…
summary: Quantum computer firms IBM, PsiQuantum and Quantinuum are pushing hard to deliver scalable systems over the next few years.
